chunks: Then I said to him: May the moaning women moan over you, O Aqil!
Do you cry on account of this iron which its maker heated for his play, while he is driving me towards the fire which its Creator prepared for His wrath!
Should you cry from pain, but I should not cry from the flames?

key_terms.الثَّوَاكِلُ: Moaning women (a phrase used for emphasis or lamentation)
key_terms.جَبَّارُهَا: Its Creator / The Almighty (referring to God)
key_terms.عَقِيلُ: Aqil ibn Abi Talib, brother of Imam Ali

ai.seo_question: What is the meaning of Imam Ali's comparison between worldly pain and the fire of Hell in Nahj al-Balagha?
ai.summary: In this poignant address to his brother Aqil, Imam Ali (peace be upon him) employs a rhetorical contrast between the triviality of worldly discomfort and the gravity of divine retribution, urging Aqil not to complain about minor hardships while Ali bears the weight of leadership and impending judgment. This passage, found in the chapter on poverty and patience, underscores the Shia virtue of *sabr* (patience) amidst political and economic hardship, reflecting Ali's unique status as the 'Gate of the City of Knowledge' who endures suffering for the sake of justice. The metaphor of 'iron heated for play' versus the 'fire of the Almighty's wrath' serves as a powerful reminder of the transient nature of material life compared to the eternal reality of the Hereafter.
